articles.title: A teen, a fiancé and a ‘fearless’ father of 2 are among the service members killed or missing in the Iran war
articles.summary: Tyler James Feehan’s greatest adventures awaited on the other side of his deployment: getting married, earning an MBA and finishing law school, his loved one...
articles.body:
Tyler James Feehan found a way to live life to the fullest, but some of his greatest adventures awaited him on the other side of his deployment: getting married, graduating with an MBA and finishing law school, his family and university said.

Now, instead of upcoming nuptials, Feehan's loved ones are making funeral arrangements for the 25-year-old – one of 19 US military fatalities that occurred amid the war in Iran .

The first service member deaths in the war came on March 1, when six Army Reserve troops were killed in an Iranian strike on a makeshift operations center in Kuwait.

Days later, an Army sergeant died after sustaining injuries during an attack in Saudi Arabia and six more service members were killed when a US Air Force KC-135 Stratotanker refueling aircraft crashed in Iraq.

In March, President Donald Trump said meeting with some of the fallen soldiers' families at the time did not give him pause about the war . He and senior officials made clear there would likely be more casualties. Indeed, the human cost of the conflict has climbed, with a wave of service member deaths in July.

Two US soldiers were killed in Iranian strikes in Jordan on July 17, and a third is believed to have been killed after being previously listed as missing.

On July 19, another service member died during a controlled detonation of a downed one-way attack drone in northern Iraq.

About 100 US service members have suffered some level of injury since July 7, according to the Pentagon, which has been slow to disclose non-fatal attacks.

At least 3,375 people have been killed in Iran since the US and Israel began strikes on the country on February 28 , according to the state-run Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting . One strike reportedly killed at least 168 children.

As families of service members still deployed overseas wait anxiously for the war to end, those who have lost loved ones are mourning the lives marked by purpose beyond the uniform.

Known by loved ones as "Tivo," Feehan was looking forward to marrying his partner after his deployment. He also planned to go to law school as another way to serve others. His family said he quoted "Legally Blonde" often, saying: "What, like it's hard?"

Feehan, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, died July 18 in Jordan, the Department of Defense said. He was assigned to 2nd Battalion, 55th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 32nd Army Air Missile Defense Command in Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

"Every day, he would come home and tell me stories about his soldiers," his fiancée, Claire Fletcher, said in a statement obtained by CNN affiliate KUTV . "Their accomplishments, their struggles, and how proud he was of them."

From climbing up to Everest Base Camp to trekking El Camino de Santiago from France through Spain, Feehan was "always looking forward to the next big adventure," his family said.

He enjoyed "building LEGO sets, cheering for the Atlanta Falcons, using Dr. Squatch soap and drinking Shatto Milk from Missouri," according to Fletcher.

Feehan was just weeks away from completing his MBA at Southern Utah University , the school said in an online statement. His degree will be awarded posthumously, the university said.

The family is working to establish a scholarship in Feehan's name to help current and future service members continue their education – a goal he also had for himself.

"We are so proud of you Tyler, completely devastated but so so proud," the family wrote in a joint statement. "We could not have asked for a better son and will make our mission to continue your legacy."

Feehan, who admired fictional soccer coach Ted Lasso, planned to become a high school football coach following his service, Fletcher said.

Feehan is survived by his parents, his partner, two sets of grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins.

The last text message Feehan sent his fiancée before he died said, "I love you," she recalled.

"I will love him for the rest of my life, and I will do everything I can to honor the legacy he leaves behind," she said.

Isabella Gonzales just graduated from high school last spring before enlisting in the Army, her Texas high school told CNN.

The 19-year-old from Carrollton, Texas, died in the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base strikes in Jordan on July 17, the Department of Defense said.

In her late teens, Gonzales exuded a level of self-confidence many spend their whole lives trying to find, her friend Jade Pena told CNN.

At Hebron High School in Carrollton, about 25 miles northwest of Dallas, the pair talked to Army recruiters together, Pena said. While Pena chose a different career path, Gonzales enlisted. They last spoke June 19 when Gonzales told Pena she was being sent to Jordan, she said.

Gonzales was assigned to 1st Battalion, 57th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade, 10th Army Air Missile Defense Command in Ansbach, Germany, the Department of Defense said.

"No matter where life took her, she never stopped being herself," Pena said. "She remained kind, genuine, and full of light. I miss her so much."

Gonzales' former school district said it was humbled by the soldier's service and the devotion to her country.

"Not long ago, Isabella walked the halls of Hebron as a student, a classmate and a friend," the Lewisville Independent School District said in a statement. "Her decision to serve after graduation speaks volumes of her character."

In the face of crisis, Angel Rampersad was the calm, her aunt Judy Rackal said at a news conference in Queens, New York.

Rampersad – or Sarah, as she was known to family – was born in Trinidad and came to the US as a toddler. She and her sister were raised by a single mother in Ozone Park, New York, her aunt said.

"She had a quiet strength, even as a child," Rackal said.

Rampersad enjoyed playing softball and bowling competitively in high school. At 18, she knew exactly what she wanted to do with the rest of her life: serve the country that helped her family make a home, according to her aunt.

"Even though she wasn't born in the US, she loved it so much that she was willing to defend it with her own life," Queens Borough President Donovan Richards said at the news conference.

She enlisted in the US Army in March 2019, serving as a signal operations support specialist in Hawaii and then Germany, the Department of Defense said in a statement.

Rampersad was killed in the July 17 Iranian strikes on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, the US military said.

"My daughter was a good soldier," Rampersad's mother, Carol Acevedo, said, fighting through tears. "She fought for this country and she died for this country, and I am a mother that is highly proud of her."

News of Rampersad's death has left loved ones both in New York and Trinidad reeling. Her father, who still lives in Trinidad, is making arrangements to travel to the US.

New York State Assemblywoman Jenifer Rajkumar expressed her condolences on Facebook , writing Rampersad "embodied the very best of the United States Army and of our country. She served far from home, stood in harm's way, and carried out her duty with honor."

Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of Fayetteville, North Carolina "answered the call to duty with courage, honor, and selfless dedication," the Department of Defense said.

To his family, Swinton was "a big teddy bear" who loved to effortlessly crack jokes and spend time with his 4-year-old daughter, his widow Mia Gonzalez- Swinton told CNN's Erin Burnett.

Swinton, "who took great pride in his work and the people around him," was kil﻿led in northern Iraq on July 19 during a controlled detonation of a downed one-way attack drone at Erbil Air Base, the Department of Defense said.

A month earlier, Swinton had sent his wife a text, saying: "If I die, just make sure that my kids know that I love them." Three days before his death, he saw his family for the last time on an unusually early morning video call, but he "sounded different" his wife said.

"He said that he loved me. He wanted to talk to our daughter, and he was asking me if I was okay," she said.

The US Army Space and Missile Defense Command said it "is saddened by the loss of Sgt. Swinton, whose death occurred during an operation to safeguard fellow Soldiers."

Sgt. Swinton was assigned to D Battery, 2nd Battalion, 55th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 108th Air Defense Artillery Brigade in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. He will receive the Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge and will be posthumously promoted to staff sergeant, according to the Department of Defense﻿.

Though Swinton was a homebody, he made plans with his loved ones in anticipation of his return home. He wanted to go on a family vacation, fishing and meet with friends, his widow said.

"He wanted to make more memories," Gonzalez- Swinton said.

After more than 100 hours of search-and-rescue efforts spanning 14,000 square miles of the Arabian Sea, the US Navy suspended operations on July 5 for Cmdr. Gabriel Edwards, commanding officer of Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 5. After Edwards' helicopter went down, the military said there was "no indication the emergency was caused by hostile action."

Edwards, a husband, father of two and "fearless leader," was a native of Oakland, Oregon. He graduated in 2006 from Norfolk State University with a degree in physics and commissioned through the Naval ROTC, according to the US Navy.

His wife Rebecca expressed gratitude for all the support and determination dedicated to bringing her husband home.

"To those who served alongside him, he was a respected leader and mentor," she wrote in a joint statement with the US Navy. "To our family, he is the love of my life, an extraordinary father to his children, and the foundation of our home. His greatest joy was always his family."

Edwards may have been soft spoken, his high school social studies teacher and track coach Jeff Clark told CNN. But he was well respected by those he led.

"Gabe was just a wonderful young man and it showed through his ascension through the military and the great job he did there," Clark said.

When asked if he has a favorite memory of his son, father John Klinner pauses.

"Gosh, there's so many," he told CNN. "Alex and I did a lot of camping trips. He loved the outdoors, and so we would go up to North Carolina every summer for years and just camped at this beautiful place. I've got a lot of good memories from those trips."

Klinner, a beloved husband and father of a 2-year-old and 7-month-old twins, was "the perfect son, the perfect child," his mother Mary Ellen said.

Just one day earlier, Klinner's parents visited their grandchildren, who will now grow up without a father. "We're heartbroken that he won't be there for them," John Klinner said. "He loved those children."

Klinner served as a major in the Air Force for eight years, his family said. As the 99th Air Refueling Squadron's chief of standardization and evaluation, Klinner oversaw the training and flight proficiency of more than 30 aircrew members, helping prepare pilots for missions, according to the Air Force.

The death "has left an immeasurable void in the lives of all who knew and loved him," according to a GoFundMe page to support Klinner's family.

"He was just very devoted to his family and community and to the Air Force. He loved flying, he was very passionate about that," his father said. "He loved life. He was just a wonderful person and cared about others and always put others before himself."

For Ariana G. Savino, flying was more than a job. It was her greatest passion, alongside mentoring "the next generation of youth, women, and minorities" in aviation and military service.

The 31-year-old was a "fierce, brave, passionate" woman with a smile and laugh that could transform the atmosphere of any room she entered, her family said in a statement shared with CNN affiliate KOMO News after she was killed in the Iraq crash.

Savino, of Covington, Washington, served as chief of current operations for the 99th Air Refueling Squadron, overseeing the unit's daily flight schedule and coordinating its training and missions, according to the Air Force.

She earned her wings as a KC-135 pilot after completing her training last year but had been serving in the military since 2017, working her way up from standardization and evaluation officer to flight commander, the Air Force said.

As a Puerto Rican, Savino was "very, very proud of her heritage" and came from a family of service members, her friend retired Lt. Col. Ernesto Nisperos told CNN.

Savino had a sweet but strong personality, Nisperos said, and had followed in the footsteps of her father, who was a pilot for Alaska Airlines.

"In a lot of ways, you know, she was trying to be like dad. It was important for her to continue a legacy in her family," he said.

Her family is starting an aviation scholarship for Latino youth and women who are interested in aviation, Nisperos said, to honor Savino's mission to be a role model and help people with the same dream she had.

Just a day before he was killed in the Iraq crash, Tyler Simmons told his father he didn't think he was coming back, Charles Mylo Simmons said in an interview with CNN , recalling their final conversations before his son's death.

"And I told him 'I'm praying for you' … I really was hoping that he was going to be wrong."

He said his son "loved what he did, he loved his country, he loved the military," and he "loved his family."

"His smile would light up the room," he said. "His personality would illuminate the whole place."

Simmons, a military boom operator, was their only child, and his mother had once hoped he would choose a different path than the military, according to WBNS.

But his passion and drive for aviation were evident early on, his father said. Teachers, he recalled, often described him as well-mannered and disciplined, and as he grew older he became increasingly focused on his goals.

"Knowing Tyler, if he could do it all over again, he'd probably make the same decision, because he loved what he did," Charles Mylo Simmons said. "He was just an amazing son and it was my privilege to be able to be his father."

Fighting back tears, Ashley Pruitt's husband told The Associated Press he had one word to describe his beloved: "radiant."

"If there was a light in the room," Gregory Pruitt said, "she was it."

Now, he and their two young children are left to carry that light forward after the 34-year-old boom operator of Bardstown, Kentucky, was killed in the Iraq crash.

Pruitt, who was based at MacDill Air Force Base, served as an instructor boom operator and assistant flight chief of operations with the 99th Air Refueling Squadron, where she oversaw training and readiness and instructed fellow boom operators in the precise mechanics of midair refueling, the Air Force said.

While she had dedicated nearly a decade to the military, rising steadily through the enlisted ranks, "nothing compared to the love she held for her family," her obituary read.

"She was a devoted wife and a deeply loving mother, and those closest to her knew she was living in her happiest chapter," it said. "Her strength, warmth, and unwavering devotion created a home filled with love and laughter."

Seth R. Koval, 38, was living his lifelong dream of becoming a pilot and wore the uniform with purpose.

He first enlisted as a machinist with the Indiana Air National Guard in 2006 and "soon discovered a calling beyond himself," according to his obituary. While serving, he earned a bachelor's degree in aviation operations from Purdue University in 2011 and later transferred to the Ohio Air National Guard in 2017.

Koval was a seasoned combat pilot before he was killed in the Iraq crash and was responsible for training pilots in "worldwide air refueling, aeromedical, cargo and passenger operations," his Air Force biography says.

His awards and decorations included the Meritorious Service Medal, Air Medal, and Air and Space Achievement Medal, the Ohio National Guard said.

His wife, whom he met on a childhood church mission trip, wrote on Facebook Koval was "many things — loving, generous, kindhearted, smart, devoted, a fixer of all things, a real outdoorsman, and selfless."

"He always put others before himself — until the very end. I will see him in the smile of our son and carry him with me in every moment," Heather Nichole said.

As the son of a flight attendant and a private pilot, Curtis Angst seemed to be destined for flight, Rep. Dave Taylor of Ohio said in a tribute to the fallen captain.

He grew up playing with toy airplanes outside his Ohio home and his father took him up for his first flight when he was still a toddler, Taylor said.

The 30-year-old, who was part of the crew killed in the Iraq crash, earned a bachelor's degree in aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati in 2014 and joined the military the following year as a vehicle maintenance technician, according to the Ohio National Guard.

Angst earned his undergraduate pilot training in 2022 before achieving his pilot initial qualification in 2024. He was previously deployed in 2015 to support Operation Spartan Shield, the guard said.

His awards and decorations included the Air and Space Commendation Medal, National Defense Service Medal and the Meritorious Unit Award, according to the Guard.

"He was always ready to help someone else before himself. His constant smile and instantly recognizable laugh made people feel welcome, valued, and part of something bigger," his obituary said.

Even as thousands of miles kept him away from his family in Iowa, Declan Coady stayed in touch with them by playing video games and talking for hours about anything from anime to his plans for the future.

The 20-year-old from Des Moines, Iowa, had been sending his family updates about his safety while in Kuwait so they knew something was wrong when the updates suddenly stopped, his sister Keira Coady told CNN.

"I wish I had called him one more time and told him I loved him," Keira Coady said, following her brother's death after an Iranian strike at Kuwait's Shuaiba port.

Declan Coady was a gym enthusiast, a fencer and an Eagle Scout with a love for﻿ camping in national parks, hiking, white-water rafting and exploring the outdoors with his family, according to his sister and his obituary.

He also loved his job in the Army Reserve, even when he worked around the clock while overseas, his father, Andrew Coady, told The Associated Press.

Declan Coady enlisted in the Army Reserve in 2023 as an Army information technology specialist. Among the youngest in his class, Coady stood out to his instructors and had been recommended for a promotion, according to his father.

"He was very good at what he did," his father said. The soldier had received several military awards, including the Army Service Ribbon, National Defense Service Ribbon and Overseas Service Ribbon.

Cody Khork's life was largely defined by three things: devotion, character, and service.

Behind his sense of duty, he was a man "known for his infectious spirit, generous heart, and deep care for those who served alongside him and for everyone blessed to know him," his family said of the 35-year-old from Lakeland, Florida.

He was among the group of six service members killed after an Iranian strike in Kuwait.

In 2009, he enlisted in the National Guard as a multiple launch rocket system/fire direction specialist. He attended Florida Southern College, where he was a member of the Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity and was known in the school community for his "leadership, character, and commitment to serving others," the university said in a statement.

Khork loved history and had a degree in political science, which showed "his sharp mind and his sincere appreciation for the principles and sacrifices that have shaped our nation," his family said.

After graduating from college in 2014, Khork was commissioned as a military police officer in the Army Reserve and was later deployed to Saudi Arabia, Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, and Poland.

His awards and decorations include the Meritorious Service Medal, Army Commendation Medal and Joint Service Achievement Medal.

Nicole Amor, a 39-year-old mother to a high school senior and a fourth-grader, was just days away from returning home, her husband said.

"She was almost home," Joey Amor told The Associated Press . "You don't go to Kuwait thinking something's going to happen, and for her to be one of the first – it hurts."

The soldier, of White Bear Lake, Minnesota, enlisted as an automated logistics specialist in the National Guard in 2005. She transferred to the Army Reserve a year later and deployed to Kuwait and Iraq in 2019.

She was an avid gardener and enjoyed inline roller skating and bicycling with her kids, the AP reported.

"Nicole believed deeply in caring for others and in nurturing life wherever she could," her obituary read.

To carry her spirit and continue her love for gardening, her loved ones raised funds to build a greenhouse and also created a foundation to build "spaces for the community to come together offering acts of service."

Those who were close with Noah Tietjens knew it was rare to see him with a smile, but looks are deceiving, some of his friends told CNN.

"He was the kind of man who represented service, humility, leadership, and heart in everything he did," said Faith Melegrito, co-owner of the Bellevue, Nebraska, studio where Tietjens spent his free time.

Martial arts were a big part of his and his family's lives. The 42-year-old earned a double black belt in Taekwondo and Filipino martial arts and was an instructor. His wife and son also practiced.

Parallel to his dedication to martial arts was his commitment to the military and mentoring. He enlisted in the Army Reserve in 2006 as a wheeled vehicle mechanic. He was in his third deployment to Kuwait and had been there in 2019 with Amor.

Army Staff Sgt. Jonn Coleman, a fellow Nebraska soldier, told CNN affiliate KETV Tietjens' mentorship was the reason he was able to advance his military career.

"He took me under his wing and got me to where I needed to be," Coleman said.

Tietjens' awards and decorations also include the Meritorious Service Medal, Army Commendation Medal and Army Achievement Medal.

Raised on a farm near Coggon, Iowa, Jeffrey O'Brien grew into a man of many passions: family, faith, jazz music and sports.

The 45-year-old husband and father of three was also known for his unwavering loyalty, especially to the Chicago Cubs, according to his obituary .

He was killed in Kuwait while serving in support of the 1st Theater Sustainment Command, which oversees the resupply and sustainment of troops across the Middle East, the Pentagon said.

O'Brien had served in the Army Reserve for nearly two decades and received several awards but he was most proud of his children.

He loved coaching them in track, cheering at gymnastics meets, and teaching them music and theater. "Many evenings and weekends were spent at ballfields, competitions, and events, creating memories his family will carry forever," his obituary said.

"He was not only a role model to our kids, but also a goofy and silly dad, always looking for ways to make the kids laugh," his family said in a statement to CNN affiliate KCCI .

"We are in shock, grieving, and grappling with the reality that we have lost the most important man in our lives, and we are trying to come to terms with how we move forward," the family said, calling O'Brien a "true hero in every sense of the word."

Robert Marzan, 54, was a mentor to young service members and often brought others in front of a whiteboard to help them "map out a life plan."

"As I reflect, Rob was probably one of the best humans I've ever met," said Connor Kuehl, a friend who met Marzan after enlisting in 2013. The late soldier helped him finish school and push him to advance in his career, Kuehl told CNN affiliate KCRA.

Marzan, from Spotsylvania, Virginia, was assigned to the 103rd Sustainment Command in Des Moines, Iowa.

He served in the military for decades, first enlisting in the Army in 1990 and deployed to Croatia, Bosnia, Egypt and Kuwait throughout his career, according to the Army Reserve.

Outside of being a soldier, his sister, Elizabeth Marzan, wrote in a Facebook post he was a loving husband, father, brother, uncle and friend.

At the time of the strike, Robert Marzan was in the final two months of his deployment and his family was planning a celebration for his 55th birthday and the end of his military service, Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa said on Facebook.

Benjamin "Ben" Pennington 's path to the military began early as he played Army with friends, watched the Military Channel and spent his days in a room decorated with Army prints and model planes hanging from the ceiling.

"Everyone who knew Ben well knew he was destined to be an Army man, and there was no convincing him otherwise," his family said in the 26-year-old's obituary .

Pennington, of Glendale, Kentucky, died on March 8 after sustaining injuries in an attack by Iran on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia. He was assigned to 1st Space Battalion, 1st Space Brigade, a unit within the Army's Space and Missile Defense Command.

He enlisted in 2017 when he was 18 as a unit supply specialist and was posthumously promoted to staff sergeant, the Army said.

Outside the military, Pennington embraced hobbies and interests that kept him closely connected to home and family, according to his obituary .

A fan of Major League Baseball, ﻿he hoped to visit each of its ballparks. While stationed at Fort Carson in Colorado, he developed a love for hiking, snowboarding and skiing, and spent time exploring the state's mountains with friends.

During trips home to Kentucky, his family said he enjoyed visiting bourbon distilleries and building his bourbon collection in recent years.

Bianca C. Wilkerson, who lived in Sumter, South Carolina, enjoyed hiking, off-roading and spending time with her family in Virginia, according to the US Army.

The 37-year-old native of Norfolk, Virginia, died on September 18 "as a result of a non-combat related incident," the Army said. She was aboard a flight to the Middle East when she began to feel unwell. An autopsy is pending, the Army said.

Wilkerson, who was supporting overseas operations in Qatar, was posthumously promoted to major, according to the Army. The incident is under investigation.

A graduate of the Virginia Commonwealth University, Wilkerson was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the US Army Reserve as a transportation officer in 2013.

She held a bachelor's degree. In the Army Reserve from 2014 to 2017, Wilkerson was the executive officer for the 678th Transportation Company in Newport News, Virginia, the Army said.

Her active duty assignments included stints as executive officer for H Company (Forward Support), 3rd Battalion, 41st Infantry Regiment, 1st Brigade, 1st Armored Division, as well as transportation and fuel officer for the 501st Brigade Support Battalion, 1st Brigade, 1st Armored Division.

After completing the Combined Logistics Captains Career Course in Fort Lee, Virginia, in 2019, Wilkerson's assignments included the 25th Division Sustainment Brigade, 25th Infantry Division, according to the Army. She was also company commander for E Company (Forward Support), 29th Engineer Battalion, 3rd Brigade, 25th Infantry Division and assistant supply officer for the 3rd Brigade, 25th Infantry Division.

Wilkerson was reassigned in 2023 as company commander for the Southern California Recruiting Battalion's Huntington Beach Recruiting Company. Two years later, she became the G4 supply and services chief for Headquarters, US Army Central & Third Army at Shaw Air Force Base, South Carolina.

Her awards include the Meritorious Service Medal, Army Commendation Medal, Army Achievement Medal (1 Oak Leaf Cluster), Army Superior Unit Award, Army Reserve Component Medal, National Defense Service Medal and the Army Service Ribbon, according to the Army.

In South Carolina, Wilkerson lived with her German Shepherd, Beau, and her boxer, Brody.

articles.title: In 2022, a career coach began helping laid-off workers search jobs for free; four years later, his volunteer network has helped more than 50,000 people

articles.body: Phyl Terry’s Never Search Alone movement has grown from a free job-search effort into a large volunteer network supporting people through unemployment and career changes. Started in 2022, the programme was built around a simple idea that job seekers should not have to handle the process by themselves. By 2026, the organisation said it had helped more than 50,000 people and launched thousands of Job Search Councils, where people searching for work support one another. The programme remains free and relies heavily on volunteers, while Terry funds it partly through proceeds from his book.Never Search Alone guided more than 50,000 job seekersPhyl Terry, a career coach and founder of the movement, developed Never Search Alone from his long experience of helping people with jobs and promotions. As reported by Remote-First Coaching, Terry had spent 20 years coaching around 2,000 job and promotion seekers before developing the approach.The idea was to change the experience of looking for work from something largely individual into a shared process. Rather than expecting people to repeatedly submit applications and wait for responses, the programme encourages them to work alongside other job seekers and make use of personal connections.Terry’s own website, Phyl.org, describes Never Search Alone as a free, global, volunteer-led movement for people who have been laid off or let go. By summer 2026, the site reported more than 50,000 job seekers helped, around 5,000 volunteers and more than 5,000 Job Search Councils launched.What happens inside a Job Search CouncilA central part of the programme is the Job Search Council, a small support group made up of people who are looking for work at the same time. Remote-First Coaching explains that a typical council has 4 to 6 job-seeking peers who agree to search together.The groups are intended to provide both practical and emotional support. Members can discuss their progress, help each other stay accountable and share what they are learning while searching for work.The programme also gives members a wider community beyond their own council. Its resources include tools and templates, videos, LinkedIn Live events and a Slack community where job seekers can communicate with others taking part in the movement.According to Never Search Alone’s website page, thousands of these councils have been launched and millions of hours of volunteer time have been invested in the community.Never Search Alone transforms the traditional job searchThe method focuses on understanding what a person actually wants before they begin applying widely. Remote-First Coaching describes a tool called the Mnookin Two-Pager, which helps job seekers set out what they enjoy and dislike doing, their requirements for a job, career goals, strengths and weaknesses.Another part of the process is the Listening Tour. This involves speaking with people to understand the job market and identify where a person's skills may fit. One of the key prompts used during these conversations, asks how someone would approach the job search if they were in the candidate’s position.The programme also includes a Job Mission with objectives and key results, designed to help job seekers understand what a potential role involves and whether it matches what an employer is seeking.The programme expanded its reach during difficult job marketsThe movement has continued expanding as different groups of workers have faced job losses. In January 2026, Terry spoke to Georgetown University’s Pivot with Purpose community about job-search strategies, networking and ways of dealing with the strain of a prolonged search.The movement later expanded its outreach to government workers. Its website page reports that from July 2025 it was offering its free safety-net programme to government employees facing job losses across federal agencies.By 2026, Terry was still running the movement and looking for additional volunteers. His own website reports the long-term aim is to make the free programme widely available to people experiencing job loss.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Germany's relationship with India has assumed greater importance amid growing global uncertainty, with the two countries looking to deepen
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Germany's relationship with India has assumed greater importance amid growing global uncertainty, with the two countries looking to deepen cooperation in trade, defence and labour mobility, German ambassador to India, Jasper Wieck, said at a press conference Wednesday.He said Germany was ready to sign an $8 billion deal with India for building six next-generation conventional submarines. "In terms of documents, it has already been finalised and the German side has agreed to it. It is now up to the Indian side to complete and conclude its internal processes," Wieck said, adding Germany was ready to sign the agreement as early as tomorrow.The agreement will see TKMS, the German defence contractor that will supply advanced submarine design and technology transfer, partnering with India's MDL.Describing the current global situation as an "era of unpredictability", Wieck said Russia had "wrecked trust and peace" while US was "constantly changing the rules of the game", making closer cooperation between India and Germany more important.Wieck assumed charge as Germany's ambassador to India and Bhutan recently.Asked about his three priorities as ambassador, Wieck identified the pending formal signing of the India-European Union FTA, labour migration, and defence cooperation.On India's continued purchase of Russian oil, he said Germany understood the energy needs of a country of 1.4 billion people but argued that reducing purchases of Russian oil would dent Moscow's ability to finance the war in Ukraine. "If we don't buy any oil anymore from Russia then financing for the (Ukraine) war stops," he said.On pending student visa issues, he said Germany was working to address the issue.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Como avatares de IA viram máquinas de ganhar dinheiro nas redes | G1
articles.standfirst: De falsos médicos a perfis românticos, 'pessoas' criadas com ferramentas atraem milhões de seguidores no país. Enquanto canais faturam com cliques, especialistas alertam para o avanço de golpes e desinformação.
articles.summary: De falsos médicos a perfis românticos, 'pessoas' criadas com ferramentas atraem milhões de seguidores no país.
articles.body:
Falsos humanos são construídos com ferramentas de IA e atuam com produção em escala industrial, com roteiros adaptados para diferentes idiomas — Foto: Reprodução / TikTok

"Ela não existe, mas paga meu cartão todo mês". "Tenho um plano infalível para o milhão". As frases, retiradas de tutoriais publicados nas redes sociais, expõem a engrenagem de um mercado em ascensão no Brasil e no mundo: o dos avatares gerados por inteligência artificial (IA).

Embora não existam no mundo real, esses personagens hiper-realistas acumulam milhares de seguidores em redes como TikTok, Youtube e Instagram, atuando como vendedores, influenciadores e até falsos especialistas, transformando canais automatizados em um negócio lucrativo.

Os produtores ganham dinheiro de diferentes formas: monetização de vídeos, comissões sobre vendas em marketplaces, divulgação de produtos digitais e até a valorização de perfis que posteriormente podem ser revendidos ou utilizados para outros objetivos em razão do alto engajamento.

Diferentemente dos chatbots, os influenciadores de IA simulam pessoas reais e interações humanas em vídeos, lives e anúncios. Em alguns casos, promovem produtos de saúde, oferecem conselhos ou divulgam tratamentos sem comprovação científica.

Fernando Ferreira, pesquisador do NetLab da Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) e doutor em IA, explica que a estratégia consiste em converter a atenção dos usuários em receita.

Com o suporte dos algoritmos, que direcionam os vídeos a públicos específicos, a produção desses avatares chega justamente a usuários que procuram respostas para problemas específicos ou demonstram interesse em determinados temas.

Já com ferramentas de automação cada vez mais acessíveis, a produção ganhou escala industrial.

"Antes a automação era só um ato de curtir, compartilhar, agora pode dar voz, pode dar imagem, então isso é uma coisa mais personalizada e mais difícil ainda do usuário conseguir identificar que aquilo é realmente uma campanha, por exemplo, alguma coisa nesse sentido", afirma Ferreira.

Mapeamentos realizados pela organização Ctrl Z mostram que os nichos de atuação variam de conteúdos históricos (como o período escravocrata) e infantis a narrativas apelativas, como a de um suposto fazendeiro viúvo em busca de uma esposa. No entanto, a manipulação de sentimentos básicos é o elemento comum a todos eles.

"Todos eles, de algum jeito, têm uma coisa muito em comum que é mexer com o medo das pessoas, com a curiosidade, com a esperança. Nos de saúde tem essa coisa do senso de urgência. Tipo: faça isso agora, não faça isso, compartilhe com alguém", aponta Luã Cruz, diretor de litigância da Ctrl Z.

Segundo Cruz, a produção em massa utiliza o mesmo roteiro traduzido para diferentes idiomas e encenado por dezenas de avatares sintéticos. Em tutoriais publicados nas plataformas, criadores desses perfis citam que um único roteiro pode ser traduzido e encenado por 20 avatares diferentes para atingir países e públicos distintos.

No YouTube, por exemplo, a estratégia serve também para cumprir os requisitos de monetização (como as 4 mil horas de exibição exigidas e mil inscritos) por meio do envio massivo de vídeos genéricos conhecidos como slop – conteúdos de baixa qualidade gerados por IA. Para Cruz, o slop não necessariamente é esteticamente ruim, mas são "IAs mal feitas" em relação às informações, com erros históricos e desinformação, e que utilizam conteúdos sensacionalistas para atrair públicos vulneráveis.

Atingida a meta , o canal pode ser redirecionado para outros nichos, com aposta em infoprodutos (como a venda de ebooks de receitas para curar determinadas doenças) ou até vendido para uso em campanhas políticas.

O impacto mais grave, contudo, recai sobre a saúde. "Vemos uma série de comentários de pessoas que de fato existem e que falam que estão seguindo aquele tratamento, que abandonaram o tratamento tradicional para seguir, enfim, aquele tratamento que [a IA] sugere", diz o integrante da Ctrl Z.

Se antes imperfeições em mãos, vozes robotizadas ou cenários distorcidos denunciavam a natureza sintética do vídeo, o avanço tecnológico reduziu drasticamente essas falhas. Diante de conteúdos consumidos em telas pequenas de celular, os especialistas dizem que transferir ao usuário a responsabilidade de checar a veracidade do material tornou-se inviável.

"Em um olhar mais atento ainda conseguimos ver se há sincronia entre a voz e a boca. São imagens muito brilhantes, é uma coisa ainda um pouco robotizada, menos do que já foi, mas ainda tem uma coisa meio robotizada. Mas são coisas muito imperceptíveis", diz Cruz.

"Cada vez vai estar melhor. Tem alguns detalhes, como observar um texto que não fica bem formatado no fundo, coisas milagrosas também. Uma pessoa que você nunca viu na vida e agora virou um influenciador", diz Ferreira. Mas ele pondera: "acho que a responsabilidade não é do usuário final. A gente tem que entrar em uma maneira de monitoramento e de clara intenção das plataformas de indicar que aquilo ali é um conteúdo de IA".

Os especialistas defendem uma sinalização obrigatória (e em destaque) para esse tipo de conteúdo, além de uma atuação das plataformas na moderação de conteúdos monetizados que são gerados por IA para proteger os usuários de manipulações e evitar crimes.

Para os especialistas, a responsabilização deve recair sobre as empresas de tecnologia. Atualmente, a maioria das plataformas exige apenas uma autodeclaração do criador indicando o uso de IA, sem mecanismos de verificação eficazes.

"A plataforma em si não é responsabilizada se está vinculando o conteúdo porque ela diz: ‘eu não tenho como saber, quem tem que dizer é o usuário'. Mas quem está fazendo a divulgação, quem está fazendo o canal é a própria plataforma. A ação de recomendação do conteúdo é da plataforma. A plataforma tende a passar a responsabilidade para a ponta, e dizer assim: ‘eu me protejo disso dizendo que ele não pode fazer, mas se ele faz e eu recomendo, paciência'. Então é esse o problema", afirma Ferreira.

Do ponto de vista jurídico, o uso de ferramentas avançadas não isenta os criadores de responsabilidade criminal. A advogada e especialista em cibersegurança Gisele Kauer destaca que a atuação de perfis sintéticos pode se enquadrar da mesma forma em crimes já previstos no Código Penal Brasileiro, como estelionato, fraude, exercício ilegal da medicina e falsidade ideológica. "O crime continua sendo crime independente do meio utilizado."

Além dos impactos financeiros e jurídicos, a proliferação desses avatares hiper-realistas criados por inteligência artificial transforma a percepção da realidade. Diogo Cortiz, professor da PUC-SP e que lidera um grupo que pesquisa intimidade artificial, aponta que a criação de padrões estéticos inalcançáveis e de interações afetivas simuladas pode aprofundar a insegurança humana, afetando tanto quem consome o conteúdo, como também quem produz.

Para ele, a IA é uma "caixa de multiversos" capaz de fabricar realidades paralelas que intensificam distorções sociais já iniciadas pelas redes sociais, como no caso dos famosos filtros utilizados em fotos.

"Começamos a criar realidades que são verossímeis, que poderiam ser possíveis, mas que não são. E isso traz uma certa insegurança, um certo desejo muito maior do que a gente tinha antes", diz o professor e pesquisador. "Temos modelos, influencers, com um corpo perfeito que é anatomicamente quase impossível chegar nele, tudo feito por inteligência artificial. Então, se a gente já se comparava com uma realidade produzida por pessoas que eram reais, imagina com uma questão sintética?", indaga ele.

Para a advogada, o problema não é o uso de personagens de IA em si para ganhar dinheiro, mas a utilização deles para induzir usuários ao erro e obter vantagens financeiras ilícitas.

Procurado, o YouTube informou que todo conteúdo na rede, incluindo o gerado por IA, deve seguir as diretrizes da comunidade, o que inclui regras contra desinformação médica, que proíbem dados incorretos capazes de gerar danos à saúde.

A plataforma também disse que exige que criadores divulguem o uso de mídia alterada ou sintética fotorrealista e que insere rótulos nesses vídeos para alertar os espectadores. "Embora dependamos da autodivulgação do criador, o YouTube usa tecnologia e análise humana para identificar conteúdos que deveriam ter sido rotulados, mas não foram", afirmou a empresa, ressaltando que pode aplicar os avisos de forma proativa nos casos em que o criador não faz a autodeclaração.

O Youtube diz, ainda, que materiais que violam as diretrizes estão sujeitos à remoção e que o descumprimento recorrente pode levar à exclusão do conteúdo e à suspensão do canal do seu programa de parcerias (YPP).

O TikTok, em resposta à DW Brasil, também afirmou que exige que criadores sinalizem conteúdos gerados por IA e disse que proíbe vídeos que induzam o público ao erro. A plataforma disse também disponibilizar rótulos para informar aos espectadores quando um conteúdo foi criado com o uso de IA. Já em relação à monetização, o TikTok afirma que perfis que violarem as regras podem ter a conta removida de forma permanente ou temporária do Programa de Recompensas do Criador, dependendo da gravidade da violação.

A Meta , responsável pelo Instagram e pelo Facebook, informou que não iria comentar.

articles.title: Body in 9 pieces, 'left for India', 'unwell' messages: Mystery shrouds Karnataka man's death in UAE as wife, son remain missing
articles.summary: UDUPI: The family of a man, allegedly murdered in the UAE and his body cut into nine pieces and packed into two bags, has sought a probe into his death.
articles.body: UDUPI: The family of a man, allegedly murdered in the UAE and his body cut into nine pieces and packed into two bags, has sought a probe into his death. The victim’s wife and their teenage son, a Class X student, are untraceable.Anil Prashanth Kunder said his younger brother, Alwin Prakash Kunder, 51, was murdered in July. His body was found in the boot of his Toyota abandoned on a road leading to Oman.According to the family, Alwin last contacted them around July 20. Messages were subsequently sent from his phone stating he was unwell and resting. But, the family became suspicious as Alwin usually communicated through voice notes and rarely typed messages.Victim’s kin get death cert, but not FIR copyWhen we questioned him and asked him to make a call, there was no response after that,” Anil said.The family contacted one of Alwin’s classmates in Sharjah, who visited the apartment provided by his company. A watchman allegedly told him Alwin had left for India. The company’s HR department initially informed the family he had travelled to India. However, after the family pointed out that he had not arrived, passport records were checked and reportedly showed he was still in UAE, he said.A complaint was filed in Sharjah. The family was later informed a body had been recovered. According to Anil, Alwin’s body was found on Aug 12. His identity was confirmed through DNA matching. The family received Alwin’s death certificate, but is yet to obtain a copy of the FIR.Alwin had been married to Tina Kunder for around 20 years. The couple have a son studying in class 10 in Dubai, while Tina worked as a schoolteacher there, according to the family.The family said they have been unable to contact Tina and their son. They claimed CCTV footage from the apartment showed two men and a woman moving luggage. However, they had no definitive information on whether Tina had been questioned by UAE police.“We cannot say anything conclusively without the FIR copy. Reports indicate they may have left for India on July 26 or 27,” Anil said.Udupi SP Hariram Shankar said Alwin’s brother had submitted a petition seeking assistance. “Unless a letter rogatory, red-corner notice or any Interpol notice is issued against the accused, there is no legal measure to be taken by Udupi police at this point,” he said.Police are facilitating contact with Dubai consulate so the family can coordinate on the investigation. “We will seek information regarding the same through Interpol channels,” the SP said.Stay updated with the latest Mangaluru news. articles.title: Eight sailors assigned to US carrier group that fought in Iran war attempted suicide, Navy secretary tells Congress
articles.summary: Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a period that included when the ships undertook com...
articles.body:
EDITOR'S NOTE: This story contains discussion of suicide. Help is available if you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters. In the US, call or text 988 for help. The International Association for Suicide Prevention and Befrienders Worldwide have contact information for crisis centers around the world.

Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a period that included when the ships undertook combat operations against Iran and the carrier set a modern record for its time at sea, according to a letter from the service's acting secretary, which was obtained by CNN.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao revealed the number, which has not been previously reported and covers crew members from several ships that travel together, including the carrier, in written responses to questions posed by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln's crew. Cao wrote that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment.

The rate of suicide attempts among the Lincoln strike group's sailors was roughly consistent with that of the entire active duty Navy in 2024, the most recent year for which the Pentagon has released suicide data. That year, the Navy saw 356 suicide attempts among its estimated 337,000 active duty sailors.

"Since the beginning of Lincoln's deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group," Cao wrote to Gillibrand, a Democrat and member of the Senate Armed Services, in a letter dated Tuesday. "This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons."

Between 6,000 and 7,000 US Navy sailors were deployed as part of the Lincoln strike group across roughly a half dozen ships — with the carrier kept out of port for over six months while conducting a high rate of combat operations against Iran.

"Eight attempted suicides is incredibly high," one US military official told CNN, noting recent carrier strike group deployments have had one or two per year. "The strain of combat ops is much higher than normal deployments. No port calls, constant alerts, etc."

The Navy did not respond ahead of publication to a request for comment about the letter.

"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday to CNN. "Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable."

The Lincoln deployed with various mental health resources onboard, including five chaplains, one embedded integrated prevention counselor, one psychologist, one clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and one expeditionary facility dog, according to Cao's letter.

CNN previously reported that two sailors assigned to the Lincoln strike group , one from the carrier and one from another ship, had jumped overboard in recent months. Both were rescued, US officials said. Others were prevented from jumping, according to reports from the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.

In his letter to Gillibrand, Cao also confirmed that a sailor assigned to the airwing went overboard from the ship in early August but was "quickly recovered" and treated by the Lincoln's medical department. "Additionally, one sailor attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to homeport."

The Navy previously said in a statement to CNN, "We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member's well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise."

A US official also previously told CNN that the Navy does not believe there is a correlation between deployment length and thoughts of self-harm, and that man overboard incidents are not unique to this group.

A crew member serving on the Lincoln previously described to CNN that morale on the carrier was very low and said they had heard repeatedly about suicidal ideation by fellow crew members. And there were regular strains on essential amenities — toilets and water fountains around the ship frequently closed, and hot water was often unavailable, the crew member said.

"Everyday we wake up and listen to our captain speak, we are desperately hoping and anxious for updates on our return," the crew member, speaking before the ship had been ordered to return to its home port in San Diego, told CNN. The ship left the Middle East in August and is expected back in San Diego in the coming weeks.

Other sailors aboard the Lincoln who spoke with CNN described conditions unlike their prior deployments, largely due to the combat that has kept the carrier from making stops at friendly ports. Ships can take on new supplies and allow their sailors to rest and relax during those port calls.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN's Davis Winkie and Pamela Brown contributed to this report.

articles.title: Kabul-Islamabad tensions soar: Pakistan strikes 10 sites in Afghanistan after drone attacks
articles.summary: Pakistan said early Thursday that it had carried out airstrikes on 10 sites in Afghanistan that it said were used to launch drone attacks against Pakistan.
articles.body: Pakistan said early Thursday that it had carried out airstrikes on 10 sites in Afghanistan that it said were used to launch drone attacks against Pakistan.Pakistan's information minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes targeted sites linked to what Pakistan described as attempted attacks from Afghan territory. He said the strikes were “deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate” and limited to military objectives.The announcement came after Pakistani officials said Afghan Taliban forces had launched eight rudimentary drones and shelled Pakistani border posts after Pakistani troops foiled what they described as an attempted cross-border infiltration by militants.There was no immediate response from Kabul to the latest Pakistani strikes. Taliban government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid had denied on Wednesday that Afghan Taliban forces carried out attacks against Pakistan.Pakistan accuses Taliban of backing militantsAccording to four Pakistani officials, the attempted infiltration took place near Afghan border posts in Paktia and Nangarhar provinces. The militants were described by Islamabad as Fitna-ul-Khawarij, a term it uses for the Pakistani Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).The officials said Afghan Taliban forces allegedly provided support to the militants and later fired mortars and other heavy weapons at Pakistani border posts after the infiltration attempt was thwarted. Pakistani forces responded with artillery fire targeting Taliban border posts, mortar positions and defensive sites.The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the latest escalation publicly, said some Afghan Taliban positions were subsequently abandoned and that there were casualties. The accounts could not be independently verified.Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Taliban government of allowing militants to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul has denied the allegations.Pakistani officials also said eight drones launched from Afghanistan were shot down before they could reach Kohat and the border town of Torkham. They said the drones caused no damage.Escalation threatens mediation effortsThe latest confrontation follows Pakistani airstrikes on eastern Afghanistan on Monday, which Islamabad said targeted militant hideouts. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, while Afghan authorities reported at least three civilian deaths and four injuries. The UN mission in Afghanistan confirmed the civilian casualties, and Kabul formally protested the strikes.The latest fighting threatens mediation efforts by China, Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which have been seeking to ease tensions between Islamabad and Kabul.The escalation also follows a series of deadly militant attacks in Pakistan's north-west. Six Pakistani security personnel were killed in a shootout with militants in Hangu, while a suicide bombing and subsequent gunbattle at a police compound in nearby Kohat killed at least 21 people.You use AI every day. articles.title: While Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens built their Texas dream mansion, Biles used a 3,998-sq-ft home as a temporary base; with the custom build finished, the 1-acre property is now listed for $1.2 million
articles.summary: Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens are moving on from the Texas home that served as their base while a much larger custom residence was being built.
articles.body: Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens are moving on from the Texas home that served as their base while a much larger custom residence was being built. The four-bedroom property in Spring, Texas, is now listed for $1.2 million after the couple completed construction on their long-awaited dream mansion. Built in 2019, the contemporary home covers 3,998 square feet and sits on more than an acre in the gated Benders Landing community. Realtor.com reports that the residence features two primary suites, a media room, private study, wine wall, three-car garage and a resort-style outdoor setting. Biles, whose name appears on the deed alongside her mother, Nellie, and Owens used the property during a period of frequent travel between Texas, Chicago and other locations. Now that their custom home is finished, the temporary base has entered the luxury property market.A temporary home during constructionThe Spring, Texas, property served an important practical purpose for Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens. While the couple worked on their custom-built mansion outside Houston, they needed a comfortable home that could function as a base for everyday life.Construction on the larger residence began in 2022 and continued for about three years. During that period, the couple’s professional commitments required frequent travel. Biles continued her gymnastics career and public appearances, while Owens played in the National Football League.The temporary property offered stability while work continued on the dream home. Instead of living around construction crews or waiting for every stage of the custom project to be completed, the couple could settle into a finished residence with space for work, guests, pets and relaxation.Realtor.com reports that the home was purchased during the construction period and is now being offered for $1.2 million. With the custom mansion complete and the couple officially settled there, the Spring residence is no longer needed as their main Texas base.Details of the Spring residenceBuilt in 2019, the home measures 3,998 square feet and includes four bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms. It also has a three-car garage, making it suitable for a household that values both space and privacy.The property sits on more than one acre inside the only gated section of Benders Landing, according to the listing. It has no rear neighbours, an arrangement that gives the home a more secluded atmosphere than many suburban properties.The listing describes the residence as a private resort designed for year-round entertainment. That description is supported by the property’s layout, which combines large indoor spaces with outdoor areas intended for hosting and relaxation.The home also includes two primary suites. This feature gives the property flexibility for owners who want separate private spaces, a guest suite or accommodation for family members.Its location provides convenient access to Houston, The Woodlands Mall and nearby golf courses. That combination of privacy and proximity likely helped make the home useful as the couple balanced a demanding sports schedule with the construction of their permanent residence.An open and contemporary interiorThe interior follows a contemporary design, with soaring ceilings and floor-to-ceiling windows bringing natural light into the main living areas.The open-concept layout connects the family room, kitchen and dining area. A modern fireplace serves as a focal point in the living space, while large sliding glass doors create a visual link between the interior and the outdoors.The kitchen features a waterfall island, quartz countertops, custom cabinetry and modern appliances. A hidden pantry provides additional storage while keeping the main kitchen area visually clean.The design appears intended to feel polished without becoming overly formal. Large windows and glass doors make the outdoor setting part of the home’s daily experience, while the open floor plan allows the space to accommodate both family life and entertaining.The listing also mentions a large dining area, making the kitchen and adjoining rooms suitable for gatherings. For a high-profile couple with family, friends and professional visitors, that flexibility can be as important as the number of bedrooms.Spaces for work and entertainmentAlongside the main living spaces, the property includes a media room and a private study.A media room can serve as a home theatre, gaming area or informal space for watching sporting events. For Biles and Owens, both of whom work in highly visible sports careers, a dedicated entertainment room would provide a comfortable place to watch competitions away from the public eye.The private study offers a quieter setting for administration, calls, planning and remote work. Professional athletes often have business commitments that continue beyond training and competition, so an office can be an important part of a modern home.The residence also has a custom wine wall with a refrigerator. While that feature adds a luxury touch, it also contributes to the home’s entertainment-focused identity.Together, the media room, study and wine wall give the property more variety than a standard four-bedroom residence. The home is designed not only for sleeping and eating but also for hosting, working and spending long periods indoors.A primary suite with resort touchesThe primary suite is designed as a private retreat. It includes two walk-in closets and a spa-inspired en suite bathroom.Dual walk-in closets provide separate storage areas and may be particularly useful in a household with demanding travel schedules and extensive wardrobes. The bathroom adds to the retreat-like atmosphere, using luxury design cues that appear throughout the property.A resort-style primary suite can be especially appealing to buyers who want their home to feel like a destination. Instead of relying on a separate holiday property, owners can enjoy privacy, space and high-end finishes within their everyday residence.That broader resort theme is also visible in the home’s outdoor layout and natural light. The property combines private interior spaces with an open connection to the surrounding grounds.The result is a home that feels spacious without depending entirely on its square footage. The design uses height, glass and connected living spaces to create a larger visual experience.A pet-friendly detailOne of the property’s more distinctive features is a mudroom with a dedicated pet-washing and feeding station.The detail may have been particularly useful for Biles and Owens, who have shared aspects of their home life and have pets. A specialised mudroom can help keep outdoor dirt away from the main living areas while creating a practical space for feeding and grooming animals.Luxury homes often focus on dramatic features such as pools, theatres or wine rooms. Smaller details can sometimes reveal more about how a property is meant to be used. A pet-washing station suggests that the home was planned for daily routines, not simply prepared as a display property.The mudroom adds another layer of convenience to the home’s design. It provides storage, separation and functionality near the entrance, while the pet area reduces the need to carry grooming equipment through the main rooms.The move into the custom mansionConstruction on Biles and Owens’ larger Texas property was completed in November, according to Realtor.com. However, the couple did not officially move in until February, after they finished packing up their Chicago residence following the end of the Bears’ season.The custom mansion had been a long-term project. During the build, the couple moved between locations as Owens’ football career developed. Biles also travelled regularly while construction continued.Once settled into the new home, Biles began sharing glimpses of the interior. One notable feature was the primary bedroom, which she said was designed to feel like a luxury hotel.In a video, she showed remote-controlled curtains opening to reveal the outdoor patio and pool. She explained that she had asked interior designer Diamond Hadley to create a hotel-like atmosphere, and said the result matched her vision.The bedroom reflects a broader approach to the custom home. Rather than creating a purely formal mansion, the couple appeared to prioritise comfort, privacy and a sense of daily indulgence.Personal touches in the new houseBiles has also used the new mansion to display important moments from her gymnastics career.Her private office includes framed memorabilia, including her January 2025 Sports Illustrated cover after she was named the magazine’s 2024 Sportsperson of the Year.Another Sports Illustrated cover features Biles alongside Michael Phelps and Katie Ledecky after the 2016 Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro. A poster from the Gold Over America Tour completes the collection.These items give the home a personal dimension. The property is not just a luxury space with large rooms and expensive finishes. It also contains reminders of Biles’ career, achievements and identity outside the competition arena.The memorabilia allows the office to function as a private gallery. It records a career that has included Olympic success, world titles and an enduring influence on gymnastics.For Biles, the new home appears to be both a retreat and a place where her professional history can remain visible.Life between Texas and IndianapolisAlthough the couple’s main home base remains in Texas, Owens’ football career has created another layer of travel.After signing a one-year deal with the Indianapolis Colts, Owens moved to Indianapolis for team activities and training. Biles told People that she expected to join him there later, while continuing to hold on to the lakefront mansion outside Houston.The couple had faced a similar arrangement during Owens’ time with the Chicago Bears. Biles travelled between Illinois and Texas while construction on the custom mansion continued.That experience may have influenced the way the couple used the Spring property. A home near Houston provided a reliable base while Owens’ career required him to spend time in another state.With the temporary property now listed, the couple may use rentals or another short-term arrangement during the NFL season. The finished mansion, however, remains the long-term centre of their life in Texas.From temporary base to luxury listingThe Spring home’s listing marks the closing of a transitional chapter. For several years, it offered Biles and Owens a finished place to live while their much larger project took shape.Now the property is being presented to a new buyer as a complete contemporary home. Its four bedrooms, two primary suites, media room, study, wine wall, private grounds and three-car garage give it the features expected in the upper end of the market.The $1.2 million asking price reflects the combination of size, location, privacy and custom finishes. It also places the home within a competitive luxury market near Houston and The Woodlands.For the next owner, the property will not be a temporary solution. It will be a substantial home designed for entertaining, working and relaxing throughout the year.For Biles and Owens, however, it represents something different. It was the place that supported their household while they waited for their Texas dream mansion to become real.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: A 1934 British sports car spent 40 years hidden in a barn; in 2026 it sold for £62,000 after bids started at £500
articles.summary: A rare 1934 Crossley Streamline spent 40 years hidden in a barn before being sold for £62,000 at a 2026 auction.
articles.body: A rare 1934 Crossley Streamline spent 40 years hidden in a barn before being sold for £62,000 at a 2026 auction. The classic car, one of only two known to exist, was among seven rare pre-war vehicles discovered in a Cambridgeshire barn and later offered by Humbert & Ellis Ltd. Bidding for the vintage car started at just £500 before more than 100 bids were placed by international buyers. The barn-find classic car still carried its original registration plate, ANB 487, and was described as a vintage concept car conceived by Sir Denniston Burney. The auction generated worldwide interest in the rare vehicle.How a £500 opening bid turned into a £62,000 saleThe auction began with bidding at £500. There were 100 bids from people overseas, highlighting the international interest surrounding the car during the auction. The vehicle eventually sold for £62,000. According to Cambridgeshire Live, bidding started at £500 and then increased, with more than 100 bids from eight international buyers. The auction was online by Humbert & Ellis Ltd, and the bidding continued through extensions in the online auction.According to Classic Car Insurance, only 25 Crossley Streamline cars were built, and just two were said to remain in existence. The car had been hidden in the barn for four decades before being brought to auction. It was one of seven vehicles found in the barn and later offered for sale. This production figure is not stated in Cambridgeshire Live's original report, which says only that the car is "one of only two known to exist.The Crossley Streamline was still carrying its original registration plate, ANB 487. The car was a vintage concept car conceived by Sir Denniston Burney, who also helped design the R100 airship. According to the report, the other known surviving example is held by Lord Montague of Beaulieu.Seven rare pre-war vehicles were found in the same barnThe Crossley Streamline formed part of a collection of seven rare pre-war vehicles discovered in the barn. Cambridgeshire Live reported that the collection had been amassed over several decades. The newspaper said the seven vehicles together generated £110,000 at auction.Other vehicles from the collection also sold at the auction. Classic Car Insurance reported that a 1925 Alcyon Cyclecar fetched £19,780, while a 1935 Crossley 2L Sports Saloon sold for £10,580. The 1925 Alcyon Cyclecar sold for £19,780, a Françon Voiturette Cyclecar achieved £14,000, and a 1932 Alvis 12/50 with a dickey seat realised £12,650. The two sources name different cars beyond the Alcyon, and neither accounts for all seven vehicles in the collection, the four prices Cambridgeshire Live reports add up to £108,430, short of its stated £110,000 total for all seven cars.Rare Crossley Streamline attracted worldwide interestHumbert & Ellis auctioneer Jonathan Humbert said the Crossley had attracted worldwide interest because of its rarity. Speaking to Cambridgeshire Live, he described the car as having “the airship” of a vehicle because of its teardrop design and noted that it was more than 18 feet long.The auctioneer also described the final stages of the online auction. Cambridgeshire Live reported that each new bid extended the auction by five minutes, with the bidding continuing as further offers were made. The Crossley Streamline ultimately sold for £62,000 after starting at £500.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Arkansas mom secretly cleared $67,676.60 in family debt in 45 days while her husband had no idea; social media followers helped erase their mortgage, truck loan and bakery business debt
articles.summary: For 45 days, Erika Dison carried a secret that could change her family's financial future.
articles.body: For 45 days, Erika Dison carried a secret that could change her family's financial future. While her husband, Cody, continued their everyday life in central Arkansas, she was quietly working to erase every dollar of their $67,676.60 debt. By the time she finally revealed what she had been doing, the couple's mortgage, truck loan and bakery business debt had been cleared.In an exclusive report by PEOPLE, the 31-year-old mother revealed how an ambitious personal challenge turned into a social media movement involving thousands of strangers.A debt-free goal that started quietlyDison had originally planned to become debt-free by December 31, 2027. The family's outstanding balances included the remainder of their mortgage, Cody's truck loan and a business loan Dison had taken to expand her home-based sourdough bakery, Rosie.As the PEOPLE report stated, the family carried no student loans or revolving credit card debt, and Dison's car was already paid off. Still, seeing the remaining total in one place clarified the scale of the challenge. Her motivation was tied to a larger family dream. She wanted to raise the couple's three children, ages 7, 3 and 7 months, on a small farm where they could grow up around animals and learn about food and farming. Rather than telling Cody about her accelerated plan, Dison created secret TikTok and Facebook accounts and began documenting her progress.Turning social media into micropaymentsDison, who has an accounting background and a strong interest in numbers, created a system that linked her social media activity directly to debt payments. Every follower, like, comment, share and save on her videos represented a dollar amount she would put toward the family's balances. She tracked the numbers in a small red notebook, recording the payments, remaining debt and percentage completed each day.Initially, the challenge was entirely self-funded. Money generated by Rosie's weekly preorders, farmers markets, events, the Little Pink Bread Shed and stores carrying her products went toward the debt.About a week into the challenge, followers began asking how they could support the effort. Dison responded by opening a Shopify store selling sourdough starter, recipes and merchandise, while supporters could also contribute through GoFundMe, Cash App, PayPal and Venmo.Strangers become the mountain moversAs her videos attracted more attention, the online community surrounding the challenge adopted the name Mountain Movers, inspired by a biblical passage that had encouraged Dison to take on the financial challenge. The movement also expanded beyond debt repayment. Through a program called Bake It Forward, followers could sponsor bread, cookies and brownies that Dison would distribute locally to people experiencing food insecurity. The purchases generated bakery income while allowing the online community to support a local cause. And behind the scenes, however, Cody remained unaware.Dison continued to manage the challenge while maintaining the family's normal routines. She reduced spending in subtle ways, planned meals around food already in the refrigerator, freezer and pantry, and kept the children from discovering the secret.$67,676.60 cleared in 45 daysThe pressure intensified as the challenge continued, particularly on Day 35, which was Cody's birthday. By then, Dison was juggling homeschooling, caring for three young children, running the household and increasing her bakery workload. On Day 45, she finally reached the $67,676.60 target. Around $40,000 came through GoFundMe, Cash App, PayPal and Venmo. Another roughly $10,000 came from Rosie, recipe sales and Mountain Mover merchandise, with the remainder coming from the family's checking account and bakery income. Dison did not receive an inheritance or unexpected windfall and did not earn money directly from TikTok. She then sat down with Cody after the children went to bed and handed him a letter explaining the entire challenge.The reveal video later reached a much wider audience after it was accidentally posted to her main TikTok account. It surpassed 1 million views within 24 hours and approached 12 million views over five days.With the debt gone, Dison's focus has shifted toward the family's next chapter: potentially building a forever home, expanding their farm dreams and helping other families find their own way through financial challenges. The Mountain Movers community that grew around her secret is now turning its attention toward helping others tackle their own financial goals, the exclusive report concludes.Image Courtesy: istock and PeopleYou use AI every day.
