articles.title: In 2007, a rare Atari game surfaced at a garage sale; 19 years later, it sold with its original cassette for $6,562.50
articles.summary: A rare Christian-themed Atari 2600 game that surfaced at a garage sale in 2007 has sold at auction for $6,562.50.
articles.body: A rare Christian-themed Atari 2600 game that surfaced at a garage sale in 2007 has sold at auction for $6,562.50. Red Sea Crossing, released through mail order in 1983, was offered by Heritage Auctions with an accompanying audiocassette. The sale marked the first time the cassette itself had been presented at auction, according to the auction house. Steve Schustack created the game and takes its inspiration from the biblical story of Moses parting the Red Sea. Players guide Moses between walls of water while avoiding obstacles and the pursuing Egyptian army. The cartridge was sold at Heritage Auctions’ June 12–13, 2026 Video Games Signature Auction, where it was listed as lot 28003.The Atari game placed players in the story of MosesRed Sea Crossing was released for the Atari 2600 in 1983 by Inspirational Video Concepts. Unlike many commercial console games of the period, it was not distributed through ordinary retail channels. Heritage describes it as a mail-order release with a Christian theme. The gameplay centres on Moses crossing the Red Sea. The player must guide him between the parted waters while avoiding hazards including seaweed, giant clams and the Egyptian army. The game also includes a fish that acts as a time limit, requiring players to reach the end of the screen before it catches up with Moses. The package was unusual in another respect. Instead of being accompanied only by a conventional instruction manual, the game was originally sold with a colouring book and an explanatory audiocassette connected to the story of the Exodus. Heritage identifies the cassette as being narrated by Dale Evans Rogers.Its only known advertisement appeared in Christianity TodayThe game’s limited distribution has contributed to its rarity. Heritage states that its only marketing was an advertisement in the October 7, 1983 issue of Christianity Today. The advertisement offered the game by mail order and helped establish that the obscure cartridge had genuinely been released. The game’s existence was not widely documented for many years. A copy discovered at a Cincinnati rummage sale in 2007 became the subject of discussion among Atari collectors, who worked to identify its developer and establish whether it was an authentic commercial release. A surviving advertisement found in Christianity Today in 2011 provided important evidence that the game had been marketed in 1983. Heritage describes the title as one of the rarest commercially released console games ever produced. However, estimates of how many cartridges were made vary among historical accounts, so the precise size of the original production run remains difficult to establish.A garage-sale discovery brought the game back into viewThe 2007 discovery was significant because Red Sea Crossing had largely disappeared from public knowledge. The game was not part of Atari’s mainstream catalogue, and its mail-order distribution meant that comparatively few examples were documented by collectors. After the cartridge was found, members of the Atari community investigated its origins and connected it to Steve Schustack. Historical accounts identify Schustack as the programmer and describe the game as an independent project released through Inspirational Video Concepts. The discovery eventually led to renewed interest in the game and to the appearance of additional examples. One copy sold at auction in 2012 for $10,400, while another copy that surfaced in Philadelphia was also sold that year. The earlier sales helped establish Red Sea Crossing as a sought-after rarity among Atari collectors.The cassette made the 2026 auction unusualThe Heritage lot consisted of the Atari 2600 cartridge and an accompanying cassette. The auction house described the cassette as particularly notable because it was the first time the tape itself had been presented at auction. That distinction matters because the cassette was part of the game’s original package but has been much less frequently documented than the cartridge. The game’s historical descriptions consistently mention the colouring book and audio recording, but surviving examples of the complete package are considerably harder to trace than reproductions and loose cartridges. Heritage described both items in the lot as being in excellent condition. The cartridge and cassette were nevertheless sold untested and as-is, with no returns.Red Sea Crossing sold for $6,562.50Heritage Auctions listed the item as lot 28003 in its 2026 Video Games Signature Auction. The auction took place on June 12 and 13, with the Red Sea Crossing lot recorded as sold on June 12 for $6,562.50. Heritage’s listing records 36 bids and registered phone bidders, with a 25% buyer’s premium applying to the lot. The result adds a new chapter to the history of a game that was originally sold through a single religious-magazine advertisement, rediscovered at a garage sale and later recognised as one of the most elusive Atari 2600 releases. The 2026 sale was especially notable not simply because of the cartridge’s rarity, but because it brought an original accompanying cassette into the auction record for the first time.You use AI every day. articles.title: Wasp spider spotted in North West for first time, Chester Zoo says
articles.summary: Wasp spiders pose no threat to humans, despite their warning colours and size, Chester Zoo says.
articles.body:
A brightly coloured wasp spider has reached the north-west of England for the first time, conservationists have said.

The large black and yellow spider was recorded during a survey on Chester Zoo's estate, with a zoo spokesperson saying this was "the first time this fascinating mimic has reached the area".

Wasp spiders have only previously been spotted in the south of England but zoo bosses believe this arrival, who they have nicknamed Wendy, is a sign that climate change was impacting UK wildlife.

A zoo spokesperson said: "Despite their warning colours and size, wasp spiders pose no threat to humans."

Zoo conservationists said the wasp spider's discovery highlighted the need to make space for nature.

The discovery was made by Chester Zoo conservationists working with RECORD, Cheshire's local environmental records centre, and was subsequently confirmed by an expert from the British Arachnological Society, the zoo said.

Estate biodiversity assistant Rosie Cooper said: "I was looking out for plant species and then I saw this big, stripey, brightly-coloured spider.

"I have what you might call a healthy respect for spiders, so my first thought was 'woah' But now I think it's really cool to have found her."

The spider is among a number of species whose ranges are moving northwards as they respond to a changing climate, the zoo said.

Ruby Merriman, Chester Zoo's estate biodiversity manager, said: "We were really thrilled to find Wendy.

"She's a beautiful and fascinating species, and recording a wasp spider in Cheshire for the first time is really exciting."

She said wasp spiders were slowly moving north as their southern ranges in Europe were warming too quickly for them to adapt.

"Some conservation organisations refer to animals driven to migrate by climate change as 'climate refugees' – which is a good term," she added.

"They are moving because of human activity, and we need to make space for them."

articles.title: When the umpires disagree: 10 questions at the heart of the Election Commission row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Two of three election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions taken
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Two of three election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions taken in the full Commission's name, according to an Indian Express report.On Wednesday, a Supreme Court-bench was split on the challenge to the law used to appoint them and asked the CJI to set up a five-judge bench.Why it mattersThe row lays bare three unsettled questions about election referee: who decides, who controls the voter database, and who picks the people at the top.Also read: What would Seshan do if faced with SIR?Here are 10 questions at the centre of the controversy.1. What exactly are the 2 EC reported to have objected to?The objections concern some of the most basic functions of election administration.According to the Express investigation, Sandhu and Joshi raised issues involving changes to Form 6, used by new voters seeking registration; deletion and restoration of names during SIR; appeals against decisions restoring voters; and access to and control over the electoral-roll database. Some notes also questioned communications allegedly issued in the Election Commission's name without approval of the Commission.The EC's response is that these were inputs during decision-making, that differing opinions are natural within a multi-member body, and that final decisions ultimately had the approval of all three commissioners.2. Can ECs disagree with one another?Absolutely. The law explicitly expects that they sometimes will.Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 says Commission business should, “as far as possible”, be conducted unanimously.“As far as possible” is the key phrase here.But it immediately provides for what happens when unanimity fails: if the CEC and Election Commissioners differ on an issue, the matter is decided according to the majority opinion.With three commissioners, the mathematics is straightforward: 2-1 decides the matter.The more intriguing issue in the current controversy is different: What happens if two commissioners say an action should not have been taken without the approval of the full Commission?3. Is the CEC the boss of the other two?The CEC unquestionably has an important institutional position, but the other two commissioners are not deputies who simply report to the chief.This question was fought over dramatically during T N Seshan's tenure. The Supreme Court upheld the creation of a multi-member Election Commission and rejected the idea that the other commissioners were merely ornamental additions. Decisions could legally be taken by majority.The 2023 law reinforces the collegial structure. It says the Commission's procedure and allocation of business may be regulated through a unanimous decision, while disagreements on substantive matters can be resolved by majority.So “Chief” does not mean the CEC has an automatic casting vote over two colleagues.In some respects, the arrangement resembles a three-judge bench more than a conventional government department headed by a secretary.4. If disagreements are routine, why has this become such a controversy?Because the reported disagreement is not simply over what the Commission should decide.Some of the notes reported by the Express raise an important question: Who authorised actions to be taken in the Commission's name in the first place?In April, for example, Sandhu and Joshi separately flagged communications they said had been issued without the requisite approval of the Commission, according to the investigation.The factual question is therefore not merely whether commissioners had different views, but whether the disputed actions fell within areas requiring approval by the Commission and, if so, what approval existed.The EC says its final decisions were collectively and unanimously taken.5. Have not Election Commissioners dissented before?Yes.Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa disagreed with the majority in five Model Code of Conduct cases involving complaints against PM Modi and then BJP president Amit Shah. In some cases the Commission's final position was reached 2-1.But the current episode is not identical.The reported notes by Sandhu and Joshi relate heavily to administration of the electoral-roll system and the process by which actions were authorised, rather than commissioners being formally outvoted 2-1.And this time, the two commissioners raising concerns constitute two of the three members.6. Should EC dissent be made public?That question remains unresolved politically and institutionally.The case for confidentiality is that collegial bodies need room for frank internal discussion. Officials may become more guarded if every disagreement is immediately made public, particularly while elections are underway.The opposite argument is that disclosure can demonstrate that controversial decisions were debated rather than simply rubber-stamped.This is a practice followed by RBI and SC.At the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, the law requires publication not only of the final resolution but also how every member voted and each member's written explanation.The Supreme Court routinely publishes majority and dissenting judgments.The Election Commission has traditionally taken a different approach. The present row has therefore revived an old question: Should an institution whose law explicitly provides for majority decisions also have a formal mechanism for publishing minority reasoning?7. Why has electoral roll software become part of the controversy?Because election administration is increasingly also software administration.The law places responsibility for constituency electoral rolls with statutory officials such as Electoral Registration Officers. But modern voter rolls are maintained through interconnected digital platforms.The Express investigation reports that Sandhu and Joshi questioned growing centralisation of access to the electoral database and the extent to which local statutory officials retained control. One episode cited involved 97 Goa voters who had been found eligible by electoral officials but could not immediately be restored because the software lacked the required facility at that stage, according to the report.The EC says its digital systems operate with appropriate security safeguards and that statutory election officials retain their legal powers.8. Why SIR makes all this more consequential?The simple answer is: Scale.The Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision has involved electoral rolls across multiple states and Union Territories. More than 13 crore names were excluded from draft rolls during the exercise across 30 states and UTs.Exclusion from a draft roll is not necessarily permanent: Voters may make claims, submit documents and pursue appeals.But depriving any electorate from casting vote for any election, howsoever local, should be treated as a serious issue in any democracy. The system needs to find a quick way to rectify it.Delhi SIR exercise has created a peculiar scenario. More than 33 lakh voters have received notices over matters including “logical discrepancies”, prompting the Supreme Court to question whether some notices appeared to have been issued “mechanically” and ask whether additional filters were needed.9. What’s the row about appointing election commissioners?On September 23, Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma differed on selection mechanism of election commissioners. Justice Sharma favoured reference to a five-judge Constitution Bench; Justice Datta took a different view and emphasised that the EC must not only be independent but also appear independent. The matter is now to go before the Chief Justice for constitution of an appropriate bench.10. So, what is the larger question raised by the EC row?It is less about whether disagreement inside the Election Commission is healthy or unhealthy. A three-member constitutional body is designed to accommodate disagreement.The bigger issue is whether there are clear rules for what happens around that disagreement.It’s also about the sanctity of electoral rolls. No eligible voter should be deprived of their right to cast vote in any kind of polls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: China hawks seethe as Trump rolls out red carpet for Xi
articles.summary: China hawks on both sides of the aisle in the U.S. are seething as President Trump prepares to welcome the country’s President Xi Jinping for what is expected to be a lavish three-day state visit to Washington. Unlike with other world leaders, Trump is pulling out all the stops for his Chinese counterpart. Trump took…
articles.body:
China hawks on both sides of the aisle in the U.S. are seething as President Trump prepares to welcome the country’s President Xi Jinping for what is expected to be a lavish three-day state visit to Washington.

Unlike with other world leaders, Trump is pulling out all the stops for his Chinese counterpart. Trump took the unusual step of welcoming Xi at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Wednesday evening and will greet him again Thursday on the South Lawn for an elaborate arrival ceremony complete with B-2 Spirit and F-22 Raptor flyovers.

Critics are questioning why Trump, who has a storied history of slamming China, is rolling out the red carpet for the U.S. adversary.

“Had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), chair of the Senate Arms Services Committee, said on the upper chamber floor Tuesday evening.

Despite the criticism over the state visit, many China critics say they are not as concerned about the optics of the state visit as much as they are about the policy developments that come out of the event.

“To me, the overall arrival and presentation is one thing. It’s certainly symbolic and can matter, especially for the Chinese side,” said Andrew Harding, a policy analyst at the Heritage Foundation who previously served as Special Assistant for Asia on the National Security Council under Trump.

“But I think from an American perspective, we need to focus on the substance of the agreements,” he continued. “What matters most about determining where the president’s position is is what is ultimately negotiated during the summit.”

Some critics of Trump’s handling of China even note that Trump hosting Xi is all a part of the diplomatic role presidents must play with other foreign leaders.

“This is one of Trump’s strengths,” said Marc Short, who served as Trump’s legislative director during his first term and was also chief of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence. “He’s good at the entertaining and the hosting, and so he should do it his way.”

“I have a bigger political concern about cozying up to Mamdani this week than I do this,” Short said, referring to Trump’s visit with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) at Gracie Mansion earlier in the week.

Trump has certainly undergone an evolution of sorts on the issue of China.

When he first ran for president in 2016, Trump would repeatedly rail against U.S. dependence on China and call Beijing a threat to the U.S. economy. The president notably flipped on his move in 2020 to ban the app TikTok — which is owned by Chinese company ByteDance — for national security purposes. Trump later joined the app in 2024 and came out against efforts to divest from the company.

“In his first term, President Trump was tougher on China than any president in 50 years, from trade to freedom of navigation in the South China Sea to cracking down on decades of Chinese spying at our universities and beyond,” said John Ullyot, former National Security Council spokesperson and deputy assistant to Trump during his first term.

“Supporters worried about this week’s summit shouldn’t mistake rote diplomatic ritual for his record, and Xi, who has a long memory, knows better than to cross Trump in the final two years of his term,” he added.

A number of major issues are hanging over the September summit, including artificial intelligence, trade, the war in Iran, the proposed $14 billion U.S. arms sale to Taiwan and the potential release of other detainees held in China.

Republicans and Democratic lawmakers are already pressuring Trump to take a hard-line stance with Xi this week.

On Wednesday, the GOP-led House Select Committee on China rolled out its own video referring to Xi as “the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] leader behind some of the world’s worst human rights abuses.”

The committee’s chair, Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), earlier this week wrote a letter to Trump, urging him to take a tough stance on several issues during the visit, including China’s potential role in Iranian strikes that killed U.S. service members, artificial intelligence and semiconductors.

And last week, Republican Sens. Ted Budd (N.C.) and John Curtis (Utah) teamed up with Democratic Sen. Ed Markey (Mass.) to sponsor legislation calling on Washington to prioritize securing the safe release of U.S. citizens wrongfully detained in China, including scholar Min Zin.

This week’s visit comes months after Xi hosted Trump for an elaborate two-day state visit in May. Among the deals reached following May’s summit, China agreed to purchase a minimum of $17 billion in agriculture goods from the U.S. on an annual basis through 2028 and resumed poultry exports from the U.S. Additionally, Trump said China also agreed to buy 400-450 GE jet engines and 200 Boeing jets following the meeting.

“Trump isn’t rolling out the red carpet in supplication to Xi, he’s demonstrating the magnanimity of a leader who is confident in his negotiating position,” said Cale Brown, former State Department principal deputy spokesperson during Trump’s first administration and chair of Polaris National Security.

Trump also made some headway on the issue of detained citizens when he met with Xi in China in May. Christian Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri, whose children are U.S. citizens, was released by Chinese authorities last summer after Trump raised his case with Xi during the state visit.

“It shows that the president is going to defend the American people and that even as he is seeking some type of managed relationship with Xi Jinping, that we’re not going to allow China to engage in hostage diplomacy. We can’t normalize that,” Harding said.

articles.title: These people built utopic communes in the 1960s. Here’s what they look like now
articles.summary: Through the Back-to-the-Land movement, communes sprung up around rural parts of the US. Decades later, their aging members have dwindled, and the homes are returning to nature.
articles.body: From the 1960s to ’70s, some one million Americans, disillusioned with modern life, left their comfortable homes in cities and suburbs for a totally new way of living. Through the Back-to-the-Land movement, communes sprung up around rural parts of the country, with a large concentration in Northern California, on land that was cheap and easy to buy. People built dwellings from salvaged materials, grew their own food, and relied on alternative energy sources. These actions greatly influenced how we think about sustainability today, and laid the groundwork for more modern homesteading lifestyles. It is largely thought about as a movement that happened, not one still happening. But around five years ago, the writer David Jacob Kramer and photographer Michael Schmelling set out to find the homes still standing in NorCal, and the people still occupying them, half a century on. What they discovered ranged from weathered sheds to beautiful gems of vernacular architecture that are slowly being reclaimed by nature. The groups involved once flourished in numbers, publishing and taking instruction from a proliferation of DIY books and guides that celebrated self-building and self-sufficiency, such as the 1973 ‘bible’ of the genre, “Shelter.” The back-to-the-landers who have remained in their homes are now in their 70s and 80s. They have stayed through generational shifts, governmental conflict, wildfires, and now, face the realities of aging in shrinking communities that require laborious upkeep. In the new book, “Handmade Utopia,” Kramer and Schmelling collect more than 40 oral histories that are accompanied by photographs. “It was really important to show exactly what it looks like now for the people that really stuck it out. There were tons of people that went up there and did it for a summer or two,” said Schmelling in a Zoom call with Kramer. “Our initial impression was that this is really hard living. It’s hard when you’re 22, and it’s even harder when you’re 80.” Kramer asked Schmelling to join the project after meeting a former back-to-the-lander who showed him the house he built and lived in, which was in extreme disrepair. He was thinking of burning it down, according to Kramer, who asked if he could photograph it before he did. As the writer sought out more of the communes, he realized they were rapidly vanishing, as their occupants aged, left or passed away, and the homes abandoned or torn down. Even as the pair worked, there was loss, with a few subjects dying before the project was completed. “It motivated us to keep going, and with a sense of urgency as well,” Kramer said. Many of the structures had never been photographed, and residents were wary of visitors. Some of the longest-standing communes still exist because they didn’t have names, were hard to access, and evaded public awareness. But Kramer and Schmelling found them from word of mouth and collected their stories. One woman, Diana Wiedemann joined a lesbian commune, Trillium, in 1973, co-founding the Heartwood Women Construction company, a rare women-led carpentry group. In a different community, Dan Borghi spoke about running a portable sawmill for 30 years while his daughters grew up, attended a local high school and left for “super expensive” universities. “This place isn’t going to last. Eventually it’ll leak through the shake roof that’s on here. I probably won’t be here to see it. My daughters, I don’t know if they’ll even want this place. Maybe they’ll want to sell it,” he says in the book. “Why am I worried about it anyway? I’m going to be dead.” Hidden works of art Schmelling said that they approached each home as a work of art in its own right. During the height of the movement, there was international interest in the architecture, but as Kramer details in the book, the builders never thought of themselves as architects. Some simple homes were built primarily for function, while others converted sheds or tacked on mismatched extensions to existing spaces. More elaborate homes took inspiration from Buckminster Fuller-like domes, or flowing Art Nouveau-inspired lines. The builder Bob McKee was responsible for many of these grander spaces; he parceled out land to hundreds of people and helped owners design their residences with a distinct visual language. “I call it hippie architecture and think it’s humorous. It’s so impractical,” one anonymous resident said in his oral account. “On the other hand, some of it is really beautiful, you know?” The Back-to-the-Land movement’s design legacy isn’t just limited to architecture, as the book documents, but furniture design and other artisan crafts, and the infrastructures that supported their way of life, such as land planning, recycling and compost systems. The communities were early proponents of solar power, too, for their homes and greenhouses, as well as cannabis farming. It’s not a movement that could be easily replicated today, Kramer said, but he sees its impact everywhere, from organic farming to sustainable design. While many of the people who gave their testimonies reflected on what it meant to live in their communities, they also spoke to the realities of getting older, with lifestyles that are hard to maintain, in homes that seem to have something new broken every day. Some have had to compromise on their strict non-consumerist attitudes. According to Kramer, some joke as they’ve gotten older that Back-to-the-Land has become “more like ‘Back to Costco,’” he said. Still, the pair believe the project presents a “different view of aging,” Kramer said. “They still had a lot of conviction… they are very empowered.” One person they met left only a recipe for his burial as his story. “Ten pounds of rinsed peat moss. Ten pounds of Golden Bi Luo tea. Ten pounds of moist black earth. Ten pounds of duckweed or liverwort. Two pounds of finely ground cooked fire-pit bones and oyster shells. One pound of finely ground charcoal.” The accounts Kramer and Schmelling collected are often frank about the reality of living in the communes. And as they completed the work, Kramer said their purpose wasn’t to prove whether the movement was successful or not. “For me especially, it was the impulse that was most exciting. Is there another way to live that is more meaningful, better for the earth, more equitable, more pure, maybe more joyful?” he asked. “I think everyone has those thoughts, but the willingness or the audacity to implement an experiment was far more interesting to me.”

images.caption: An anonymous resident of Table Mountain Commune told the authors: “Back in the day, everybody used to have their own little cabin here and they all used to go up and have dinner together. People don’t all eat dinner together anymore.”
The back-to-the-landers have faced generational shifts as children have grown up and left and longtime residents have moved out or died, without new community members to replace them.

“We were in our early twenties, but we were like kids playing house,” a man known as Captain Rainbow told Schmelling and Kramer. “We could build sh-t in the woods. Because I didn’t know what I was doing, I didn’t know that some of the stuff I was doing was impossible, so I did it. It’s really weird — why is it still standing?”

An archival photograph of stained-glass artist Richard Evans in 1979. He told the authors: “We were called by this land...These trees were so tired of being abused! Like they’re just their timber, not trees, they were money. And here was a group of people who wanted to love them and care for them and be here, appreciate how beautiful this place is.”

“Everybody wanted to have the second story on their house,” said Janferie J. Stone, whose partner, Dan Borghi, built this dome. “The ability to look out into forest-scape, a little niche spot, where you could sit and read a book. We wanted to have spaces that made you feel individual and cared for.”
Back-to-the-landers designed their own kind of vernacular architecture that ranged from simple sheds to elaborate designs.
Land was cheap, and Back-to-the-Landers used found timber and upcycled materials to build their homes.
Though nature has worked to reclaim the structures over time, many of the structures still show the character of their design.
The back-to-the-land movement didn't just have an impact on architecture, but environmental policy, organic farming, and modern homesteading.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill eight people across Ukraine as US steps up diplomacy
articles.summary: US and Russia engage in urgent talks to reduce war’s impact on global energy during UN General Assembly.
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least eight people as the United States steps up diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the war.

Six people were killed and eight wounded on Thursday in a Russian attack on a farm in northern Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.

Two more people were killed in Russian attacks on Kyiv, one of them in the car park of a maternity hospital that was damaged, officials said.

The assault included an unspecified number of hypersonic and ballistic missiles, 282 drones and other weapons, Ukraine’s air force said.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it targeted Ukrainian defence sites, logistics and telecommunications hubs, and vessels used by the military.

The ministry also said its forces struck a Black Sea tanker bringing fuel and lubricants to Ukraine’s port of Chornomorsk.

In Russia, falling drone debris sparked a fire at an industrial facility in the southern region of Krasnodar, local authorities said, adding that no one was injured.

Poland’s military said it deployed planes to secure its airspace in response to the attacks on Ukraine. Two Czech fighters were also deployed to aid the effort.

“These measures are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting the airspace, particularly in areas adjacent to threatened regions,” it said in a post on X.

Poland also said a fire at a Starlink ground station in the centre of the country was deliberate sabotage aimed at cutting internet access for institutions, including the Ukrainian military.

Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski called the incident “hybrid warfare” and said that while responsibility was not established, it “aligns with Russia’s new doctrine of attack”. Moscow has denied carrying out such attacks.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski told Al Jazeera that NATO had “contingency plans” for what he called Russia’s “provocations”.

The attacks came after the US had conducted a flurry of diplomacy with the two warring nations in a bid to reduce the impact of the war on the global economy.

On Wednesday, US officials met separately with Russian and Ukrainian officials on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York to discuss the war.

Although no agreements were announced, the US invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the next Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida.

On Thursday, an international investment bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, reported that growth in developing economies was slowing, in part due to the increasing prices of energy and wheat. Ukraine is a top exporter of the grain, much of which is shipped across the Black Sea.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called for a full and immediate ceasefire in Ukraine, starting in the Black Sea, to safeguard grain and food supplies.

“Ukraine had a very good grain harvest this year,” he said in a statement. “But because of the Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports, it can’t be delivered to the world. Russia is thereby exacerbating hunger and starvation worldwide.”

The office of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said he told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea are “inexplicable” and steps must be taken on navigational safety.

Erdogan also told him that Turkiye was ready to do all it could to end the war with a lasting peace and would keep pushing to revive direct talks.

articles.body: Trump’s decision to ban three news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional, a federal judge said. Mark Zuckerberg talks AI and Meta’s new audio glasses in an exclusive interview. And Netflix turns Willy Wonka’s chocolate factory into a “social experiment.” Here’s what to know today. Judge orders White House to restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico The White House must immediately restore temporary access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, a federal judge has ordered, saying that President Donald Trump’s directive barring the news outlets was most likely unconstitutional. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. In granting a 14-day temporary restraining order reinstating the outlets’ access while their legal challenge proceeds, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their lawsuit against the Trump administration, at least on the grounds that their credentials were revoked last week without due process. Trump, he wrote, did not dispute that the outlets “did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked.” Trump had posted on social media before a Wednesday hearing in the case that he expected the “totally disloyal” Kelly, whom he nominated to the bench during his first term, to rule against him — adding that “as usual, we’ll go for appeal.” More details on Trump’s media ban and fallout. Mark Zuckerberg on Meta’s new audio glasses, Muse and if AI will kill us all Meta unveiled its latest glasses yesterday. They’re thin, without cameras and focused on all things audio. And in the past week, the company’s Muse AI agent has surged to the top of the Apple App Store. The announcements come amid intense and heated debates over whether AI development is moving too fast — and whether companies should slow it down. In an exclusive interview with NBC News’ chief tech analyst Joanna Stern, Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg said he doesn’t think there’s a need for “some kind of industrywide coordination” as long as companies take their time and address issues as they arise. Zuckerberg also brushed off the idea that AI will end humanity. Beyond the more existential questions, Zuckerberg laid out his vision for the future of computing and showed off the company’s new products. That includes the $349 Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, equipped with six microphones to allow users to listen to music, make calls and talk to AI. Zuckerberg was adamant that the camera-free glasses weren’t a response to the recent backlash about the company’s camera-equipped glasses. Meta’s $1,299.99 VR glasses can be used for watching video or as a workstation with multiple virtual screens, to name a few intended uses, and emphasizes mixing the virtual world with the real one. And the Muse AI agent is one of the first consumer-friendly agents designed to do things for you, not just answer questions. Zuckerberg predicts that “in the future, everyone’s going to have a personal agent that can basically do things for them.” But for Muse to become truly useful, Stern notes, you have to trust Meta with access to a huge chunk of your digital life. Read the full story here. And watch the complete interview. U.S. and China agree to trade truce as Xi’s state visit kicks off Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the U.S. and China will extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire in November through Jan. 10. The announcement came only minutes after Chinese President Xi Jinping touched down in Washington, D.C., for a three-day state visit. The extended trade truce resolves the main issue of today’s summit, though Bessent teased more potential announcements in the coming days. Another key issue Trump and Xi will discuss is AI, which is increasingly at the center of U.S.-China competition. Where things stand headed into the summit. More world news: Yemen’s government is seeking U.S. military support in its fight against the Houthis, a senior official said, as the Iranian-backed rebels expand their control of the Red Sea coast. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a defiant tone during his address at the United Nations General Assembly, saying the Islamic Republic would not limit its nuclear program but was open to negotiations.Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez, delivering her first address to the U.N. General Assembly since coming to power, promised elections and said the nation’s people will determine the “right moment.” Poll: Young voters view socialism more positively than capitalism Negative views among voters about capitalism have risen in the past eight years, a new NBC News survey found. But many voters remain wary of socialism, even as a populist streak grips American politics. Overall, 48% of registered voters have positive views of capitalism, the poll found, compared to 52% in 2018. And 29% of voters view capitalism negatively this year, a double-digit rise from 18% in 2018. Broad views of socialism have remained largely unchanged over the past eight years. But a look under the surface reveals shifting mindsets among subsets of voters. For those ages 18 to 29, the share of people with negative views of capitalism more than doubled from 22% in 2018 to 47% this year. And the share of voters with positive views of socialism has increased from 28% in 2018 to 42% this year. What voters said about socialist political candidates. articles.title: Did we just hear the Iranian regime’s last speech at the UN?
articles.summary: When Masoud Pezeshkian stood before the United Nations, he spoke in the name of Iran. That was the first deception. The Islamic Republic — the Shia Caliphate — is not Iran. Khomeinist ideology has been imposed upon a civilization that long predates the order established in 1979. Yet Pezeshkian carried the same exhausted script: victimhood,…
articles.body:
When Masoud Pezeshkian stood before the United Nations, he spoke in the name of Iran. That was the first deception.

The Islamic Republic — the Shia Caliphate — is not Iran. Khomeinist ideology has been imposed upon a civilization that long predates the order established in 1979. Yet Pezeshkian carried the same exhausted script: victimhood, Palestine, resistance, Israel, American hostility, and a regime perpetually surrounded by enemies.

What was conspicuously absent was Iran itself.

Where were the political prisoners, protesters shot in the streets? Where were those arrested, tortured or blinded, and families who have buried their children? Where were the millions crushed by inflation, poverty, censorship, and religious authoritarianism?

They were nowhere in his speech. Pezeshkian portrayed the Islamic Republic as a victim while ignoring its violence against Iranians. He spoke of infrastructure, but Iran’s most precious infrastructure is its people — a generation beset by repression, economic ruin, and isolation from the world.

This is the grotesque contradiction at the heart of the Islamic Republic. A notorious regime that has spent decades financing and arming terrorist groups abroad presents itself at the U.N. as an apostle of peace. A regime that suppresses dissent lectures the world about justice while branding all of its opponents as agents of America or Israel. It speaks endlessly of Gaza and Palestine while trying to hide the blood it has spilled in Iran’s streets. And still, the world is expected to call this “diplomacy.”

For decades, Washington has viewed Iran through the same narrow window: nuclear enrichment, sanctions, negotiations, terrorism, shipping, and the security of American allies. But this obscures the most consequential reality inside Iran. The central conflict is no longer simply between Tehran and Washington or the regime and Israel. It is between the Iranian nation and this cult itself. Confusing Iran with the regime that has ruled it since 1979 remains a fundamental failure in understanding the country.

Iran’s rulers understand this distinction, which is why domestic dissent frightens them so much. Their deepest fear is not diplomatic condemnation; it is a population that rejects the state’s ideological foundations and separates its national identity from the Islamic Republic.

This explains why protests terrify the establishment, communications are restricted during unrest, dissent is portrayed as foreign conspiracy and the prospect of an alternative is so sensitive for Tehran.

Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi has become a prominent advocate of a secular and democratic transition beyond the Islamic Republic. Washington cannot appoint Iran’s next leader — that decision belongs to Iranians. But American policymakers should not behave as though Iranian politics begins and ends with the Islamic Republic. Ignoring political forces advocating a post-Islamic Republic future does not make them disappear, nor does treating the clerical establishment as permanent make it so.

President Trump should understand this distinction before starting another cycle of negotiations. Diplomacy is not inherently dishonorable; states negotiate with adversaries. But negotiations that constrain a dangerous regime are fundamentally different from those that prolong its survival, replenish its resources or grant it international legitimacy.

For decades, Washington has hoped that sanctions, incentives, negotiations, or factional politics might transform the Islamic Republic into a conventional state. Yet presidents and rhetoric have changed while so-called reformists and hard-liners have traded places and the architecture of power has endured.

That is why Pezeshkian’s performance at the U.N. mattered. Beneath the denunciations of Israel, invocations of Palestine, resistance, and accusations against the U.S. stood a political system desperately trying to convince the world that it speaks for Iran. But political alienation within Iran cannot be erased by diplomacy, propaganda, missiles or repression. A regime can possess formidable security institutions while suffering a profound crisis of legitimacy.

The question for Washington is whether the U.S. is strategically prepared for the possibility that the Islamic Republic will not endure. Preparing for that future means documenting human-rights abuses, maintaining Iranians’ access to information, engaging political voices outside the ruling establishment, and planning with allies for a transition. Iran must not descend into chaos if the Islamic Republic collapses; any transition should protect its territorial integrity and institutions while preventing further bloodshed and authoritarianism.

This is the conversation Washington should be having, rather than perpetuating the illusion that the clerical order established in 1979 is an eternal fact of Middle Eastern life.

Perhaps Pezeshkian will return to the United Nations next year. Perhaps another representative of the Islamic Republic will stand behind that green marble podium and repeat the same exhausted slogans of resistance, justice, and victimhood. But history does not guarantee regimes another speech.

The U.S. heard the Islamic Republic this week; the White House should finally hear the Iranian nation. The Islamic Republic is not Iran, and it is not immortal. Behind its missiles, intelligence apparatus, prisons, and propaganda stands an exhausted and increasingly frightened political order sustained not by national consent, but by coercion. The world should begin preparing for the day after it.

Erfan Fard is a counter‑terrorism analyst and Middle East researcher based in McLean, Va.

articles.title: Israel’s Netanyahu and the Palestinian Authority’s Abbas to speak at United Nations General Assembly
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas are set to address world leaders at the UNGA. Follow for the latest updates.
articles.body:
• What we’re watching: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas will address global leaders during today’s morning session of the United Nations General Assembly. Abbas’ remarks will be via video after being denied a visa by the Trump administration.

• Against backdrop of war: Their speeches come as nearly three years have passed since the October 7, 2023 terror attacks and Israel’s subsequent war against Hamas in Gaza, leading to thousands of deaths and regional instability.

• What else has happened: In his UNGA address yesterday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will not bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin “patient zero” in his speech, saying the Russian leader spreads war and instability. Meanwhile, Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez said her country will hold elections and transition to a full democracy, but didn’t specify when.

Welcome back to our coverage of all the big developments and speeches at the UN General Assembly today.

We’re expecting speeches from both Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas today, though his remarks will be delivered remotely because the Trump administration denied visas to Abbas and other Palestinian officials.

Abbas is the fourth speaker in this morning’s session while Netanyahu, who is making a notably short trip without meeting US President Donald Trump, will speak 17th. In total, 35 countries will speak today as we steadily make our way through all the UN member states during this high-level week when the world’s leaders and top diplomats descend on New York.

However, some of the diplomatic focus will today be pulled away from New York toward Washington DC, where Chinese leader Xi Jinping is making his first state visit to the US since 2015, though few major diplomatic breakthroughs are expected.

The second day of the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly featured more speeches from world leaders, including addresses from Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez , Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian .

Venezuela’s acting President Rodríguez said Venezuela will hold elections and transition to a full democracy — but did not specify when — in her address to the UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor Nicolás Maduro.

Rodríguez thanked US President Donald Trump for “his willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation.”

She also addressed Venezuelans recovering from the devastating earthquakes that shook the country in June, saying: “Let us walk united as one nation that decided, in the wake of pain, to choose hope.”

Iran’s President Pezeshkian told the General Assembly his country will “never bow our head or bend at the knee” to the US.

He said the Iranian people have been “the victims of terrorism,” countering Trump’s speech on Tuesday, where he called the Iranians “terrorists.”

Separately, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said US-Iran talks on the sidelines of the UNGA did not yield a breakthrough.

In his UNGA speech, Ukrainian President Zelensky called Russian President Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the more freedom he has to act, “the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.”

Zelensky later said a Russian attack on Kyiv Wednesday killed at least two people, urging the international community to increase pressure on Russia to end its more than four-year war.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for reforming the UN Security Council to “ensure fair representation for all regions of the world and to end the veto power of permanent members” in his address.

Earlier, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino also proposed reforming the Security Council to grant permanent membership to countries from Latin America and the Caribbean.
